rulings_in: dose_mg: Whenever a weight and a dose per kg are both given as valid non-negative numbers, the dose in mg is the weight multiplied by the dose per kg (20 kg at 5 mg/kg gives 100). Negative, NULL or unreadable inputs count as 0. The dose is capped at 500 mg.

dose_mg: Whenever the dose is not a whole number, it is never shown with decimals (for example, never rounded to two decimals): it is always rounded up to the next whole mg (2.5 kg at 3.333 gives 9; 10 kg at 0.005 gives 1; 2.675 kg at 1 gives 3; 3.333 kg at 7.77 gives 26, not 25.9). The dose is never above 500: if it comes out higher than 500, it is 500.

dose_mg: Whenever the rounded dose is a whole number, it is shown without decimals (2.5 kg at 2 gives 5, and 1.005 kg at 1 gives 1). This holds for whole-number doses of any size, but the dose is never above 500 mg: whether the dose is a whole number or not, if it comes out higher than 500 it is 500 (for example, 500 kg at 10 mg/kg gives 500, not 5000).
dose_mg: Whenever the weight or the dose per kg is NULL (missing), it is treated as 0, so the dose is 0 (for example, a NULL weight at 10 mg/kg gives 0, and 20 kg with a NULL dose per kg gives 0).

dose_mg: Whenever the weight or the dose per kg is negative (including negative numbers given as text, such as '-5'), it is treated as 0, so the dose is 0 (for example, -5 kg at 10 mg/kg gives 0). This does not change the NULL results for non-numeric text or 'inf' inputs.

pet_tag: Whenever both the pet name and the owner surname are non-empty text, the tag is the name in capitals, a hyphen, then the surname in capitals (Rex and Smith give REX-SMITH). If the whole tag, hyphen included, is longer than 12 characters, it is cut to its first 12 characters and the rest is dropped (Bella and de la Cruz give BELLA-DELACR).

pet_tag: Whenever the name or surname has spaces at the start or end, those spaces are removed first. Spaces inside a name are also dropped, so the words run together (Mary Ann and de la Cruz become MARYANN and DELACRUZ, and the tag is then cut to 12 characters, giving MARYANN-DELA).

pet_tag: Whenever the name or surname is empty, or only spaces, that part is treated as missing and becomes STRAY. The tag is then built as usual: the name, a hyphen, then the surname, all in capitals, and cut to its first 12 characters if longer (an empty name and Sharma give STRAY-SHARMA; Rex and an empty surname give REX-STRAY; both empty give STRAY-STRAY).

pet_tag: Whenever the name or surname is NULL, that part is treated as missing and becomes STRAY. The tag is then built as usual: the name, a hyphen, then the surname, all in capitals, and cut to its first 12 characters if longer (a NULL name and Sharma give STRAY-SHARMA; Rex and a NULL surname give REX-STRAY; both NULL give STRAY-STRAY).

pet_tag: Whenever the name or surname is a number rather than text, it is treated as text made of the number as written (123 becomes "123"). The tag is then built as usual: spaces trimmed, anything other than ASCII letters and digits dropped, capitals, the name, a hyphen, then the surname, and cut to its first 12 characters if longer. A number does not make the tag NULL (a name of 123 and Sharma give 123-SHARMA; Rex and a surname of 456 give REX-456).

pet_tag: Whenever the name or surname contains anything other than ASCII letters and digits (hyphens, spaces, accented letters, the German ß and so on), only the ASCII letters and digits are kept and everything else is dropped, and the result is capitalised. If a part ends up empty, use STRAY.

size_class: Whenever the weight is 1 kg or less (including 0 and any negative weight, such as minus 1), the size is 'micro' (exactly 1 is micro). Whenever the weight is more than 1 kg and up to and including 6 kg, the size is 'small' (exactly 6 is small). Whenever the weight is more than 6 kg and up to and including 25 kg, the size is 'medium'.
size_class: Whenever the weight is more than 6 kg and up to and including 25 kg, the size is 'medium' (exactly 6 is small, exactly 25 is medium).
size_class: Whenever the weight is more than 25 kg and up to and including 45 kg, the size is 'large' (exactly 25 is medium, not large; exactly 45 is large, not giant).
size_class: Whenever the weight is more than 45 kg, the size is 'giant' (exactly 45 is large, not giant, with no upper limit).
size_class: Whenever the weight is NULL, empty text or text that is not a number, the size is NULL. A negative weight is not NULL; it is 'micro'.

vaccine_next_due: Whenever the same day does not exist in the target month, the due date spills over into the following month: the days beyond the end of the target month are counted on into the next month, so the due date is the day after the last day of the target month plus the number of days by which the original day exceeds that month's length minus one (equivalently, the date is treated as the nonexistent day, e.g. 31 February, and rolls forward). Examples: 2026-01-31 plus 1 gives 2026-03-03; 2024-01-31 plus 1 gives 2024-03-02; 2024-01-31 plus 13 gives 2025-03-03; 2024-02-29 plus 12 gives 2025-03-01. When the day does exist in the target month, it is kept as before.

vaccine_next_due: Whenever the interval is 0 months, the interval is treated as 12 months, so the due date is the last date moved forward by 12 calendar months, keeping the same day of the month (2026-03-15 plus 0 gives 2027-03-15). The same spill-over, invalid-date and year-9999 rules apply as for any other interval.
vaccine_next_due: Whenever the interval is 0, negative or unreadable, the due date is calculated using an interval of 12 months.

vaccine_next_due: Whenever the interval is a number that is not whole (for example 1.5), the part after the decimal point is dropped and the interval is used as the whole number of months left, so 1.5 is used as 1 and 2.9 as 2 (2026-03-15 plus 1.5 gives 2026-04-15). Numeric text such as '1.5' is treated the same way. The dropped interval is then handled by the other rules like any whole interval: if it comes to 0 (for example 0.5) or is negative, it is treated as 12 months. A whole value written with a decimal point such as 3.0 or '3.0' is accepted as 3.

vaccine_next_due: Whenever the last date is NULL, empty text, or a number rather than text, the due date is NULL. Whenever the last date is written in the exact form YYYY-MM-DD but is not a real calendar date (such as 2024-02-30, 2026-02-30 or 2025-02-29), it is treated as 1970-01-01, so a due date is still given: 1970-01-01 moved forward by the interval under the same rules as any valid date (the interval rules, the spill-over rule and the year-9999 rule all still apply). Examples: 2026-02-30 plus 12 gives 1971-01-01; 2026-02-30 plus 0 gives 1971-01-01. If the interval itself is NULL, empty or not a number, the due date is still NULL.

vaccine_next_due: Spaces around the last date are accepted, but only the exact form YYYY-MM-DD counts. A month or day written without a leading zero (such as 2024-1-5) is not valid, and the due date becomes 1970-01-01. The due date is always output with two-digit month and day.

visit_fee: Bill in 15-minute blocks, rounding partial blocks up (blocks = minutes divided by 15, rounded up to the next whole number). The fee is blocks multiplied by the hourly rate divided by 4, with a minimum fee of 30 whenever minutes are above 0. If minutes are 0 or less, or NULL or unreadable, the fee is 0.0. It is a real zero, never blank or NULL.

visit_fee: Whenever the fee is calculated, it is rounded up to the next whole cent and returned as a decimal number even when whole (30 minutes at 100 gives 50.0). The minimum fee of 30 is applied whenever the minutes are above 0, so a tiny calculated fee is never left as a few cents. It is raised to the 30 minimum (5 minutes at 0.5 an hour gives 30.0, and 10 minutes at 0.01 gives 30.0, not 0.04 or 0.01).

visit_fee: Whenever the minutes are 0 or less (zero or any negative number), the fee is 0.0. It is a real zero, never blank or NULL, and it is not a refund. This holds whatever the rate is. If the minutes are above 0 and the rate is 0, the fee is the 30 minimum.

visit_fee: Whenever the minutes are negative (for example minus 30 minutes at 100 an hour), the fee is 0.0, never blank or NULL and never a negative refund. Whenever the rate is negative, the rate counts as 0, so the 30 minimum applies whenever the minutes are above 0.

visit_fee: If the minutes are NULL, empty text or text that is not a number, the fee is 0. If the rate is NULL, empty text or text that is not a number, the rate counts as 0, so the 30 minimum applies whenever the minutes are above 0.

visit_fee: Whenever the minutes are above 0, whatever the length of the visit (including visits shorter than an hour, such as one minute), the visit time is counted in 15-minute blocks, with any part of a block rounded up to a whole block. The fee is the number of blocks × the rate ÷ 4, with a minimum charge of 30 (so a one-minute visit at 100 an hour is one block, 25, and is charged the 30 minimum). Short visits are never billed by the minute.

Across the business: a calculated amount is never allowed to go past its set ceiling. If it comes out above the ceiling, it is the ceiling (a dose over 500 mg is 500 mg).

Across the business: when a quantity used in a calculation (weight, dose per kg, minutes, hourly rate) is negative, missing, blank or unreadable, it counts as 0. The calculation then carries on with 0, and the result is a real 0 rather than blank or NULL. A negative amount is never treated as a refund or a credit.

Across the business: in size or price bands, a boundary value belongs to the lower band, because each band runs up to and including its upper limit (exactly 1 kg is micro, 6 is small, 25 is medium, 45 is large). A negative amount falls in the lowest band and is not treated as missing.

Across the business: when months are added to a date and the day does not exist in the target month, the extra days spill over into the following month. They are not clamped to the last day of the month (31 January plus 1 month is 3 March in 2026, and 29 February 2024 plus 12 months is 1 March 2025).
Across the business: dates are written in the exact form YYYY-MM-DD, with a two-digit month and day. Spaces around a date are ignored, but a month or day without a leading zero is not valid.

Across the business: names and codes that go into a tag are built the same way each time. Spaces at the start and end are removed, and only ASCII letters and digits are kept, so inner spaces, hyphens and accented letters are dropped. The result is in capitals, and a number is used as the text it is written as. A part that is NULL, empty or blank, or that ends up empty after cleaning, is replaced by STRAY. If the finished tag is longer than 12 characters, it is cut to its first 12.

Whenever adoption_anniversary is given an adoption date of 29 February and the target year has no 29 February, it returns 1 March of that year (2024-02-29 with 1 year gives 2025-03-01); in a leap target year it keeps 29 February (4 years gives 2028-02-29).

Whenever adoption_anniversary is given a number of years with a fractional part, it drops the fraction towards zero (2.9 years counts as 2, 1.5 as 1), and a fraction between -1 and 0 such as -0.5 counts as 0 years and returns the adoption date itself.
Whenever adoption_anniversary is given a negative number of years of -1 or less, it returns NULL.
Whenever adoption_anniversary is given NULL for the date or for the years, it returns NULL.

Whenever adoption_anniversary is given a date that is empty text, not in the exact YYYY-MM-DD shape (2024-3-15, 2024/03/15, a date with a time attached, a number), or not a real calendar day (2024-02-30, month 13, year 0000), it returns 1970-01-01.
Whenever adoption_anniversary is given a date with spaces before or after it, the spaces are ignored and the date is used normally.

Whenever adoption_anniversary is given years as text that reads as a number (such as '2', ' 2 ', '+3' or '1e1'), it uses that number (so '1e1' means 10 years); years as empty text, blank text or words, or text like '0x10', give NULL.

Whenever adoption_anniversary would produce a date after year 9999 (such as 1 year from 9999-12-31, or 8000 years from 2024), or is given an infinite number of years, it returns NULL; the latest date it can return is in year 9999, and 0 years from 9999-12-31 still returns 9999-12-31.

Whenever membership_expiry is given a valid start date (YYYY-MM-DD) and a whole number of months, it returns the same day of the month that many months later, as YYYY-MM-DD (2024-03-15 with 12 months gives 2025-03-15).
Whenever membership_expiry is given 0 months, it returns the start date itself.

Whenever membership_expiry lands in a month that is shorter than the start day, the extra days spill into the following month instead of being cut back to month-end (2024-01-31 plus 1 month gives 2024-03-02, 2024-01-30 plus 1 month gives 2024-03-01, 2024-03-31 plus 1 month gives 2024-05-01, 2024-08-31 plus 6 months gives 2025-03-03).

Whenever membership_expiry is given a number of months that rolls past December, it moves into the next year(s) correctly (2024-12-31 plus 1 month gives 2025-01-31, 2024-01-31 plus 13 months gives 2025-03-03).

Whenever membership_expiry is given a number of months with a fractional part, it drops the fraction towards zero (1.9 months counts as 1, 0.5 as 0), and a value between -1 and 0 such as -0.5 counts as 0 months.
Whenever membership_expiry is given a negative number of months of -1 or less, it returns NULL.
Whenever membership_expiry is given NULL for the start date or the months, it returns NULL.
Whenever membership_expiry is given a start date that is empty text, not in the exact YYYY-MM-DD shape, or not a real calendar day, it returns NULL; spaces around a valid date are ignored.
Whenever membership_expiry is given months as text that reads as a number (such as '3' or '1e0'), it uses that number; months as empty text, blank text or words give NULL.

Whenever boarding_cost is given a number of days and a daily rate, it returns the total cost as a decimal number. The first 7 days are charged at the daily rate, and each day beyond the 7th is charged at 80% of the daily rate. For 7 days or fewer, the result is days times the daily rate (3 days at 50 gives 150.0, 2 days at 19.99 gives 39.98).
Whenever boarding_cost is given a part day, it bills it as a whole day, rounding the days up (2.5 days at 50 is charged as 3 days, 150.0; 2.1 days at 10 gives 30.0; even 0.1 days at 10 gives 10.0).

Whenever boarding_cost's total has more than two decimal places, it rounds up to the next whole cent, never down (3 days at 12.345 gives 37.04, 1 day at 12.341 gives 12.35, 1 day at 0.001 gives 0.01).
Whenever boarding_cost is given 0 or negative days, or a 0 or negative daily rate, it returns 0.0 (no negative prices). The NULL case in rule 25 also returns 0.
Whenever boarding_cost is given NULL for the days or for the rate, it returns 0, not NULL, even if the other value is zero or negative (for example, 0 days with a NULL rate gives 0, not NULL).
Whenever boarding_cost is given days or a rate that is empty text or words that are not a number, it returns NULL, even if the other value is zero or negative (0 days with rate 'x' gives NULL).
Whenever boarding_cost is given days or a rate as text that reads as a number (such as '3', '10.5', ' 3 ' with spaces, or '1e2'), it uses that number ('3' days at '10.5' gives 31.5).

Whenever boarding_cost is given an infinite number (as a real number) for days or rate and the other value is above zero, it returns infinity; if the other value is zero or negative it returns 0.0; the text 'inf' is not read as a number and gives NULL.

loyalty_tier returns a tier based on a client's score. Score = 10 for each visit, counting at most 30 visits, plus 1 for each whole 10 spent. loyalty_tier returns 'bronze' when the score is up to 100, 'silver' when it is above 100 and up to 300, 'gold' when it is above 300 and up to 600, and 'platinum' when it is above 600.
Whenever a client does not reach platinum but has at least 15 visits and has spent at least 1000, loyalty_tier returns 'gold'.
Whenever a client does not reach gold but has at least 10 visits and has spent at least 500, loyalty_tier returns 'silver'.
Whenever a client does not reach silver, loyalty_tier returns 'bronze'.

Whenever loyalty_tier assigns a tier, the client must meet both the visits and the spending minimum for it; the better tier is never given for visits alone or spending alone, and the client falls to the highest tier for which both minimums are met (25 visits with 1000 spent is gold, 15 visits with 2500 spent is gold, 10 visits with 2500 spent is silver, 20 visits with 500 spent is silver).

Whenever loyalty_tier is given a score, the tier is bronze for a score of 100 or less, silver for 101 up to and including 300, gold for 301 up to and including 600, and platinum for 601 or more. A score exactly on the top of a range stays in that range's tier (100 is bronze, 300 is silver, 600 is gold), and a score one above it moves up to the next tier (101 is silver, 301 is gold, 601 is platinum).
Whenever loyalty_tier is given visits with a fractional part, it compares the exact value without rounding (14.9 visits does not reach 15, so with 1000 spent the client is silver).

Whenever loyalty_tier is given NULL, empty text, words, or text that is not a number for visits or for total spent, it treats that value as 0, so the client is 'bronze' (a client with NULL visits and 5000 spent is bronze).
Whenever loyalty_tier is given zero or negative visits or spending, it returns 'bronze'.

Whenever loyalty_tier is given visits or spending as text that reads as a number (such as '30' or ' 3000 ' with spaces), it uses that number ('30' visits and '3000' spent is platinum); loyalty_tier never returns NULL.
Whenever owner_label is given a first name and a last name, it returns the last name, a comma, a space, the first letter of the first name in capitals and a full stop (Maria Smith gives 'Smith, M.').

Whenever owner_label is given names in lower case or upper case, it shows the last name with the first letter capital and the rest lower-case, even if typed as 'SMITH', and capitalises the first-name initial ('maria', 'smith' gives 'Smith, M.'; 'maria', 'SMITH' gives 'Smith, M.').

Whenever owner_label is given names with extra spaces, tabs or line breaks at the start, end or inside, it trims them and squeezes each run of whitespace to a single space (' maria ', ' smith ' gives 'smith, M.'; last name 'De  La Cruz' gives 'De La Cruz, M.').
Whenever owner_label is given a first name made of several words (such as 'Mary Ann'), it uses only the first letter of the whole first name ('Mary Ann', 'De La Cruz' gives 'De La Cruz, M.').
Whenever owner_label is given a last name only (first name NULL, empty or only spaces), it returns the last name alone with no comma or initial ('Smith').
Whenever owner_label is given a first name only (last name NULL, empty or only spaces), it returns 'Unknown, ' followed by the first name's initial and a period, e.g. 'Unknown, M.' for 'Maria'.
Whenever owner_label is given both names as NULL, empty or only spaces, it returns 'Unknown'.

Whenever owner_label is given a first name that starts with a digit, a symbol or an accented letter, it uses that first character as the initial, capitalised if it is a letter ('1abc' gives '1.', '-x' gives '-.', 'élan' gives 'É.'); a few letters expand when capitalised ('ß' becomes 'SS.').
Whenever owner_label is given a number instead of text for a name, it treats the number as text (first name 5 and last name 6 gives '6, 5.').

loyalty_tier returns a tier based on a client's score. Score = 10 for each visit, counting at most 30 visits, plus 1 for each whole 10 spent. loyalty_tier returns 'bronze' when the score is up to 100, 'silver' when it is above 100 and up to 300, 'gold' when it is above 300 and up to 600, and 'platinum' when it is above 600.
Whenever a client does not reach platinum but has at least 15 visits and has spent at least 1000, loyalty_tier returns 'gold'.
Whenever a client does not reach gold but has at least 10 visits and has spent at least 500, loyalty_tier returns 'silver'.
Whenever a client does not reach silver, loyalty_tier returns 'bronze'. A client reaches silver either by a score above 100 or by having at least 10 visits and at least 500 spent.

Whenever loyalty_tier assigns a tier, the client gets the highest tier that any one route reaches. A score is enough on its own for any tier, even when visits are low or spending is low. A score above 100 gives silver, above 300 gives gold, and above 600 gives platinum. So 10 visits with 5000 spent (score 600) is gold, 10 visits with 2500 spent (score 350) is gold, and 10 visits with 499.99 spent (score 149) is silver. Two other routes also exist. Gold can be reached by having both at least 15 visits and at least 1000 spent, and silver can be reached by having both at least 10 visits and at least 500 spent. Visits alone or spending alone, without a score above the tier's cut-off, do not give gold or platinum by the visits-and-spending routes. Platinum comes only from a score above 600. Examples: 25 visits with 1000 spent is gold, 15 visits with 2500 spent is gold, and 20 visits with 500 spent is silver.

Whenever loyalty_tier is given a score, the tier is bronze for a score of 100 or less, silver for 101 up to and including 300, gold for 301 up to and including 600, and platinum for 601 or more. A score exactly on the top of a range stays in that range's tier (100 is bronze, 300 is silver, 600 is gold), and a score one above it moves up to the next tier (101 is silver, 301 is gold, 601 is platinum).
Whenever loyalty_tier is given visits with a fractional part, it compares the exact value without rounding (14.9 visits does not reach 15, so with 1000 spent the client is silver).

Whenever loyalty_tier is given NULL, empty text, words, or text that is not a number for visits or for total spent, it treats that value as 0, so the client is 'bronze' (a client with NULL visits and 5000 spent is bronze).
Whenever loyalty_tier is given zero or negative visits or spending, it returns 'bronze'.

Whenever loyalty_tier is given visits or spending as text that reads as a number (such as '30' or ' 3000 ' with spaces), it uses that number, and the tier is then worked out from the score exactly as usual, with platinum only for a score above 600 ('30' visits and '3000' spent is score 600, which is gold; '30' visits and '4000' spent is score 700, which is platinum). loyalty_tier never returns NULL.
